    AI Overview
    Appendicitis is a medical emergency caused by an inflamed appendix, usually triggered by a blockage, resulting in sudden, severe abdominal pain that often moves from the belly button to the lower-right abdomen. Symptoms include vomiting, loss of appetite, fever, and abdominal tenderness. Seek immediate care for severe pain. 
    Symptoms of Appendicitis 
    • Pain: Often begins around the belly button and shifts to the lower right abdomen.
    • Pain Intensity: Worsens with movement, coughing, or walking.
    • Digestive Issues: Nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, or diarrhea.
    • Other:
      Low-grade fever, abdominal bloating, and inability to pass gas.
    • Note: Pain may differ in children or during pregnancy. 
    Causes of Appendicitis
    Appendicitis occurs when the appendix becomes blocked by: 
    • Hardened stool (fecaliths): The most common cause, where appendix stones block the opening.
    • Lymphoid hyperplasia: Swollen lymphoid tissue, often following a viral infection.
    • Colitis or tumors: Other sources of obstruction or infection.
    • Result: The obstruction causes bacteria to multiply, leading to swelling, pus, and potential rupture. 
    Diagnosis 
    • Physical Exam: Checking for pain in the lower right abdomen.
    • Blood and Urine Tests: To check for infection or pregnancy.
    • Imaging Tests: Abdominal ultrasound or CT scan are commonly used to confirm inflammation. 
    When to Seek Medical Attention 
    • Immediately: If you or your child experience sudden, sharp abdominal pain that starts around the belly button and moves to the right side.
    • Rupture Warning: If pain temporarily improves before getting significantly worse, and symptoms include a high fever or rigid abdomen, get emergency care. 
    Risk Factors 
    • Age: Most common in people aged 10–30.
    • Sex: Slightly more common in males.
    • Family History: Family history of the condition can increase risk. 
    Treatment 
    • Appendectomy: Surgery to remove the appendix is the standard treatment.
    • Antibiotics: Sometimes used, but surgery is preferred to prevent rupture. 
    If left untreated, an infected appendix can rupture in 48–72 hours, spreading infection in the abdomen (peritonitis), which can be fatal.

    How fast does appendicitis progress?
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    Appendicitis typically progresses rapidly, with a high risk of the appendix rupturing within 24 to 72 hours after symptoms begin. Initial, mild discomfort often moves to the lower right abdomen and becomes intense within 12 to 24 hours. Seeking emergency care within the first 24-48 hours is crucial. 
    Key Stages and Timing
    • 0–24 Hours (Early Phase):
      Initial pain often starts near the belly button, accompanied by loss of appetite, nausea, or vomiting. 
    • 24–48 Hours (Progression):
      Pain typically shifts to the lower right abdomen (McBurney point) and intensifies. Pain worsens with movement, walking, or coughing. 
    • 48–72 Hours (Critical Phase):
      Risk of rupture increases significantly if left untreated, leading to peritonitis, a serious infection. 
    Important Considerations
    • Pediatric Risk:
      Appendicitis can progress even faster in children, sometimes rupturing within 24–48 hours. 
    • Symptoms of Rupture:
      If the pain suddenly subsides and then spreads across the entire abdomen, or if a high fever (e.g.,
      104∘F104 raised to the composed with power cap F
      or
      40∘C40 raised to the composed with power cap C
      )       develops, the appendix may have already burst.       
    Disclaimer: If you or someone else is experiencing severe, worsening abdominal pain, seek emergency medical attention immediately.

      How can I rule out appendicitis at home?
      An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
      AI Overview
      It is not possible to reliably rule out appendicitis at home; it requires professional medical diagnosis. While tests like the "jump test" (pain when jumping or coughing) or pressing on the lower right abdomen can suggest inflammation, any suspicion of appendicitis should warrant immediate emergency medical evaluation. 
      Signs of Possible Appendicitis
      • Pain Location: Initial pain around the navel that moves to the lower right abdomen. 
      • Movement Pain: Worsening pain with walking, jumping, coughing, or sudden jolts. 
      • McBurney's Point: Extreme tenderness halfway between the navel and hip bone. 
      • Other Symptoms: Fever, loss of appetite, vomiting, or diarrhea. 
      When to Seek Immediate Emergency Care
      Do not try to manage this at home if you experience: 
      • Sudden, severe pain that increases over a few hours.
      • High fever.
      • Pain that worsens when letting go after pressing on the abdomen (rebound tenderness).
      • Inability to pass gas or stool.
      Disclaimer: This information is for educational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice. Seek emergency care immediately if you suspect appendicitis.

        How do you check if you have appendicitis?
        Appendicitis tests may include:
        1. Blood tests to look for signs of infection and inflammation that may mean you have appendicitis. But blood tests can't diagnose appendicitis.
        2. A urine (pee) test to rule out a urinary tract infection and/or a kidney stone. ...
        3. Imaging tests to take pictures of your appendix.
